Map","treatment":"translate","rendering":""}],"translationNotes":"Many segments are duplicated (likely an animated or split-text effect) and some are split by ⟦n⟧ markers into fragments (e.g. 'I'm Lalitya ⟦1⟧Krishnan⟦2⟧.'). Translate each duplicate identically, keep the markers in place, and make sure every fragment still reads naturally when joined, reordering words only if the target grammar requires it and keeping the markers attached to the same words. Several lines are sentence openers continued in the next element: 'Product Designer at' + company logo/name, 'Master of Design from' + institution, 'Made with' / 'Designed with' + an icon (likely a heart), 'Good things start / with / a hello.' Keep these as grammatically open fragments that connect to what follows, and keep the 'Good things start with a hello' line as one warm, memorable sentence. 'Hello, there.' is a casual, friendly greeting (a playful 'Hello there'), not formal; use a natural casual equivalent. First person is the male author, so use masculine forms wherever the language marks gender, e.g. 'I design... write... cook'. The triad 'design experiences, write poetry & cook delicious food' should keep its light rhythm and the surprising pivot from work to poetry to food; keep '&' as 'and' or the local equivalent. Project blurbs are telegraphic resume language: keep them concise, parallel and verb-led, and keep numbers and metrics literal ('30 secs' = 30 seconds, reduced transaction time). Keep product, app and brand names untranslated; transliterate people, places and institutions only when the script requires it. Source typos should be silently fixed, not reproduced: 'Bancasurrance' (a heading for bancassurance, but keep it as the project's title), 'Plannogramy' / 'planogrammy' (planogram), 'it's management' (its), 'neccessity', 'Al' (should be AI), 'Visualised... and Led' stray capital, and the missing end of 'reducing onboarding time'. Translate 'planogram' consistently as the retail shelf-layout term. Domain terms like claims, garages, field driver, investigator, and claim manager should use the standard insurance vocabulary of the target market. 'Counterless' means a checkout-free, staffless store. 'Aegis' is a name, so keep it. UI strings: 'Scroll to experience' is a playful invitation (the pun on experience is optional to preserve), 'Let's talk' is a friendly button, and 'Feel free to reach out,' is a gentle lead-in to the email field. 'Made it this far?' is a cheeky, warm remark to a reader who scrolled to the bottom. 'Laiba's stalling. Click to skip' is a humorous loading message; keep the name Laiba and the joke tone (someone is slow, so the user can skip). Section headers (Industry, Academic, Creative, projects, explorations) pair across lines as one phrase ('Industry projects', 'Academic projects', 'Creative explorations'), so use matching wording. The '©' line and '·' separators stay as they are; the year 2026 stays as written. Nav items 'Work' and 'About' should be short single words.","dominantLanguage":"en"}

communities","treatment":"translate","rendering":""}],"translationNotes":"The author is male: use masculine first-person forms wherever he speaks as I (e.g. 'I started with', 'I questioned', 'I selected') in gendered languages; 'we' in 'How can we...' is the generic design-question we, not personal. Much of the page is duplicated (responsive/animated copies and stacked headings); translate identical strings identically. Headings are split across segments with ⟦n⟧ markers (e.g. 'The hidden cost' / 'of convenience'; 'Using plastic,' / 'more responsibly'; 'Questioning' / 'the initial brief'): keep the marker order and make each fragment read naturally; reorder words only if the grammar demands it, and keep the markers. The short lines 'What if, instead of simply eliminating single-use plastics, / we explored new materials... / unlocks potential...' form one sentence broken over three lines (the source has a grammar slip, 'unlocks'); translate it as a single flowing sentence across the three lines with correct grammar. The opening imagery (a toy chest that holds stories, not plastic waste; a fleeting moment of joy before landfill) is the emotional hook: keep it vivid and concrete, and do not turn it into dry report language. 'Woven themselves into daily life', 'trail of destruction', 'loom large' and 'confront head-on' are figurative: adapt them to natural equivalents rather than going word for word. Keep 'web of interconnected challenges' as a web/network image if it works in the language. Section labels (Introduction, Context, Problem, Brief, Process, Discover, Define, Develop, Deliver) appear as nav, numbered tabs and headings: use one consistent rendering for each. Keep numerals 01–09 and 1–7 as they are. Keep acronyms (NID, SDGs) as written, with a translated expansion for the UN Sustainable Development Goals. The Indian context matters (Indian initiatives, rural livelihoods, agricultural residues): keep India-specific facts and the name 'Biomanufacturing Initiative' faithful, and translate the Indian government name as an official-sounding but plain term. Mind British spelling and mixed 'utilising/utilization'; this has no effect on meaning. The tone is constructive, not alarmist: avoid heightening the environmental language. Short UI-like items (tabs, buttons, bullet list of scope) should be concise and parallel in form (verb-led: Reduce..., Raise..., Create..., Build...). The 'Revised problem statement' is a long defined question: keep its full logic and all listed qualities (inclusive, practical, economically viable, sustainable across lifecycle, positive environmental, social and economic impacts) intact. 'Patra' is the product name and also an everyday word (leaf/plate) in several Indian languages, so keep it as written in Latin script (or transliterate only if native usage is natural) and never translate its meaning.","dominantLanguage":"en"}
